notice.text: The palace closes for lunch (11:00–14:00) and may close temporarily during royal ceremonies. Shoulders and knees must be covered.

hero.title: Royal Palace of Cambodia (Phnom Penh)
hero.subtitle: A living royal residence and Cambodia's most sacred cultural landmark, where Khmer tradition meets French colonial elegance on the banks of the Four Rivers.

rows.label: Location
rows.value: Samdach Sothearos Blvd (3), Phnom Penh (plus code HW7J+HG)

about.title: About the Royal Palace of Cambodia
paragraphs: Welcome to the Royal Palace of Cambodia, widely recognized as the central Royal Palace Phnom Penh. Located in the heart of Phnom Penh, Cambodia, this destination serves as a primary hub for travelers visiting the region.

The Royal Palace of Phnom Penh was founded in 1866 by King Norodom I, who moved the capital back to Phnom Penh from Oudong. He chose this site at the confluence of the Four Rivers — the Tonlé Sap, the Upper Mekong, the Lower Mekong and the Bassac — a place Khmer geomancy regards as a protective, prosperity-bringing heart of the kingdom.

More than a museum, the palace remains the official residence of the Cambodian royal family and the stage for coronations, royal weddings and state ceremonies. Its layout blends traditional Khmer architecture with the French colonial influences introduced during the protectorate.
Did you know? When the golden royal flag flies above the palace's tallest spire, it means the reigning monarch — King Norodom Sihamoni — is inside.

timeline.title: History & Significance of the Royal Palace of Cambodia
timeline.subtitle: From a royal vision to a living heritage

events.title: Capital moved to Phnom Penh
events.desc: King Norodom I relocates the court from Oudong and begins building the palace complex.

events.title: Throne Hall completed
events.desc: The central ceremonial hall rises with its 59-metre gilded tower.

events.title: Silver Pagoda established
events.desc: A wooden sanctuary for royal relics is built; later reclad in solid silver.

events.title: Reamker murals painted
events.desc: Artists cover the cloister walls with 600 m of the Khmer Ramayana.

events.title: Restored as royal residence
events.desc: After turbulent decades, the monarchy is reinstated and the palace reopens to the public.

architecture.title: Highlights & legends
architecture.intro: Centuries of craftsmanship, faith and royal spectacle — here are the treasures you should not miss.

items.name: Throne Hall (Preah Tineang Tevea Vinichhay)
items.nameLocal: ព្រះទីនាំងទេវវិនិច្ឆ័យ
items.desc: Topped by a 59-metre golden tower blending Khmer prasat form with Brahmin symbolism. Used for coronations, receptions of foreign heads of state and royal audiences. Photography inside is strictly forbidden.

items.name: Silver Pagoda (Wat Preah Keo Morakot)
items.nameLocal: វត្តព្រះកែវមរកត
items.desc: The floor is laid with 5,329 solid silver tiles (about 1 kg each). Inside stands a life-size 90 kg solid-gold Buddha encrusted with 9,586 diamonds — the largest a 25-carat stone at the crown — and a 17th-century crystal (Emerald) Buddha said to bring peace and harvest.

items.name: The Reamker Cloister
items.nameLocal: ចម្លាក់រាមកេរ្តិ៍
items.desc: A 600-metre gallery of murals (painted 1903–1904) narrating the Reamker, Cambodia's version of the Ramayana — battles of gods and demons, apsara dancers and the loyal monkey-god Hanuman.

items.name: Chanchhaya Pavilion (Moonlight Pavilion)
items.nameLocal: ព្រះរាជបន្ទំចន្ទឆាយា
items.desc: An elegant open-air pavilion facing the avenue, historically the royal grandstand for classical Apsara dance performances and ceremonial parades.

items.name: Royal Gardens & Napoleon III Pavilion
items.nameLocal: ឧទ្យានព្រះរាជវាំង
items.desc: Shady lawns, topiary and a small iron pavilion gifted by France — a calm place to rest between sights.

visitorGuide.title: Plan your visit
visitorGuide.hoursValue: 08:00–11:00 and 14:00–17:00. Closed for lunch (11:00–14:00). May close temporarily for royal ceremonies or state events.
visitorGuide.durationNote: Go early (08:00) or after 14:30 to beat the heat and the crowds.
tips: Hire an official guide at the entrance ($10–$15) for royal stories and hidden details.
Carry USD cash — tickets are sold on-site only.
No photography inside the Throne Hall or the Silver Pagoda.
Watch the royal flag: if it flies, the King is in residence.
route: Enter at the main gate and pause at the ticket booth.
Stroll the Royal Gardens toward the Throne Hall (view the exterior and staircase).
Visit the Silver Pagoda and the 600 m Reamker cloister.
See the royal regalia, carriages and costume exhibition.

ticket.title: Tickets
ticket.notes: Includes the palace grounds, Throne Hall exterior and the Silver Pagoda. Photos are NOT allowed inside the Throne Hall or the Silver Pagoda. Bring your passport; the dress code is enforced.

dressCode.title: Dress code (strictly enforced)
dressCode.intro: The palace is an active royal and religious site. Visitors in sleeveless tops, shorts or skirts above the knee are regularly turned away — even a scarf over the shoulders may not be accepted.

items.title: Not allowed
items.desc: Sleeveless tops, shorts, short skirts, ripped jeans, crop tops, see-through fabrics.

items.title: Required
items.desc: Shoulders and knees fully covered — a T-shirt with sleeves and long trousers or a long skirt.

items.title: Comfort
items.desc: Modest, breathable clothing and comfortable shoes; you will walk outdoors in the heat.

transport.title: Getting there
transport.intro: The palace sits on Samdach Sothearos Blvd, facing the Tonlé Sap river in central Phnom Penh.

modes.name: By air
modes.desc: Phnom Penh International Airport is about 30 min by taxi to the palace.

modes.name: By tuk-tuk / taxi
modes.desc: The easiest way across town; ask for 'Royal Palace' (preah ba-rom rea-chh veang).

modes.name: On foot
modes.desc: Walkable from the Riverside, the National Museum and Wat Phnom in 10–20 min.

steps.title: From the airport
steps.detail: Take an official taxi from the airport rank (flagfall ~$12–15 USD, 30–40 min). Show the driver 'Royal Palace, Samdach Sothearos Blvd'.

steps.title: From downtown / Riverside
steps.detail: Hail a tuk-tuk or passapp (ride-hailing app); the fare is usually $2–4 USD. Ask for 'Preah Barom Reachea Vaeng'.

steps.title: By tuk-tuk to the gate
steps.detail: Ask to be dropped at the main entrance on Samdach Sothearos Blvd, facing the river — the ticket booth is just inside.

steps.title: On foot
steps.detail: If you are along Sisowath Quay, walk north ~3 min; the palace walls and golden spires are unmistakable.

gallery.title: Photo gallery
gallery.caption: Glimpses of the gilded spires, silver floors and tranquil gardens of the Royal Palace.

nearby.title: Landmarks & Attractions Around the Royal Palace Phnom Penh
nearby.intro: When visiting the Royal Palace of Cambodia, visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including the National Museum of Cambodia and the Riverside (Sisowath Quay). Make a day of the riverside quarter.

food.title: Food nearby
food.intro: Refuel along the river after your visit.

items.name: Khmer traditional
items.desc: Try amok, lok lak and beef salad at riverside restaurants.

items.name: Riverside cafés
items.desc: Shaded spots for iced coffee, fresh coconut and people-watching.

items.name: Night market
items.desc: Evening stalls for grilled skewers, noodles and tropical fruit.

photography.title: Photography tips
photography.intro: The grounds are a dream for photographers — just respect the no-flash, no-interior rules.

times.name: Morning (08:00–10:00)
times.desc: Soft light and fewer crowds; cool before the heat.

times.name: Late afternoon (15:00–17:00)
times.desc: Warm gold light on the spires; long shadows in the gardens.

bestTime.title: Best time to visit
bestTime.intro: Phnom Penh is hot year-round; plan around the heat and the rains.

seasons.note: Most comfortable; peak season, arrive early.
Very hot; visit at opening or late afternoon.
Afternoon showers; mornings are clear and green.

items.q: How much is the ticket and where do I buy it?
items.a: About $10 USD, paid in cash on-site at the entrance. Cards are generally not accepted, so bring US-dollar bills.
Strongly recommended. Official multilingual guides (including Chinese) at the entrance cost about $10–$15 and unlock royal history and hidden details.
Shoulders and knees must be fully covered. Sleeveless tops, shorts and short skirts are not allowed, and a scarf over the shoulders may be refused.
08:00–11:00 and 14:00–17:00, with a midday closure from 11:00 to 14:00. The palace may also close for royal ceremonies.
You may photograph the gardens and exteriors, but photography and video are strictly forbidden inside the Throne Hall and the Silver Pagoda.

items.q: How long should I plan for?
items.a: About 1.5–2 hours for the highlights: Throne Hall exterior, Silver Pagoda, the Reamker cloister and the royal regalia exhibition.

items.q: Where is the Royal Palace of Cambodia located?
items.a: The Royal Palace of Cambodia is located on Samdach Sothearos Blvd (3) in Phnom Penh, Cambodia (Google plus code HW7J+HG), on the west bank of the Tonlé Sap river next to the National Museum of Cambodia.

items.q: Is the Royal Palace of Cambodia free to visit?
items.a: No. General admission is about $10 USD per person and is paid in cash at the entrance; there is no free general admission.

lib.outfitWind56: Breezy conditions, so keep hats, scarves and loose items under control.

lib.outfitUv: The sun here is strong, so cover up rather than trusting shade alone.
lib.outfitMuggy: High humidity makes it feel hotter than the number suggests — choose quick-drying fabrics.
lib.outfitDiurnal: There is a real gap between day and night temperatures, so keep one light layer for the evening.
lib.outfitWarmNight: It stays warm and humid after dark, so light clothing works right through the evening.
lib.outfitCold: Cool by local standards — bring a warm layer for the early morning.
lib.outfitClear: Clear skies and strong light: excellent for photographs, hard on bare skin.
lib.outfitCloudy: Soft, even light — the best conditions of the week for photographing murals and facades.

lib.planRainHeavy: Outdoor sightseeing is not advisable during the downpour; the National Museum five minutes away is the obvious wet-weather substitute.
lib.planRain6: Front-load the outdoor courtyards and keep the indoor halls in reserve for the afternoon shower.
lib.planRainLight: Outdoor areas lose some of their appeal, so start with the cloister and the temple buildings.
lib.planWind56: River cruises and some open-air attractions may be suspended, so check before you commit.
lib.planWind7: Expect open-air and riverfront activities to close; switch to an indoor itinerary.
lib.planFog: Not a day for viewpoints — the interiors and the museum make better use of the time.
lib.planHot: Shorten each stretch outdoors and use the midday closure for shade, water and a proper sit-down.
lib.planClear: A fine day for the courtyards, and good light for sunrise or sunset over the river.
lib.planCloudy: No burning sun today, which makes a long unhurried walk through the whole complex comfortable.
lib.planWindowMorning: The morning window is much drier than the afternoon, so go early.
lib.planWindowAfternoon: Rain is more likely in the morning, which makes the afternoon window the safer bet.
lib.planWindowUv: UV peaks in the afternoon; the morning window is the gentler choice.
lib.planHours: The palace opens 08:00–11:00 and 14:00–17:00 and closes over midday — the break suits lunch and the museum.

lib.packRainHeavy: A rain jacket rather than a long umbrella — wind makes long umbrellas useless

lib.packCold: A warm coat and a scarf
lib.packClear: Sunscreen, even if the shade feels cool
lib.packFog: Allow extra buffer time for ferry, coach or flight delays

lib.tipRainHeavy: Heavy rain — plan an indoor day
lib.tipHotUv: Hot with high UV — go early
lib.tipClear: Clear and bright — good photo light
lib.tipMild: Mixed conditions — keep the plan flexible

services.title: Visitor Services & Nearby Facilities
services.intro: A category-by-category overview of the practical facilities around the Royal Palace of Cambodia — which types of service exist within walking or short-drive distance, and how they usually work.
services.neutralNote: This guide is non-commercial and does not name or recommend individual businesses. Establishments and opening conditions change frequently, so treat the notes below as general categories and confirm details on site.

items.title: Toilets & drinking water
items.text: Public restrooms are available near the entrance area and beside the Silver Pagoda. Tap water in Phnom Penh is not drinking water; bottled water is sold by small shops around the entrance and along the riverside.
items.tip: Use the restrooms before you enter the interior courtyards — facilities inside the grounds are limited.

items.title: Parking
items.text: There is no large dedicated car park. Cars generally use paid or marked street parking along Samdach Sothearos Blvd and the surrounding blocks, and tour coaches stop at designated curbside points. Motorcycle parking is easier to find close by.
items.tip: Ride-hailing apps and tuk-tuks avoid the parking question altogether, especially at peak hours.

items.title: Food & drink
items.text: There is no full-service restaurant inside the grounds. Within a five to fifteen minute walk you will find a wide range of local restaurants, cafés, bakeries and street-food stalls, concentrated in the riverside quarter.
items.tip: Budget stalls, mid-range dining rooms and upscale places sit side by side — compare a couple before committing.

items.title: Accommodation
items.text: The immediate palace district is a low-rise historic quarter with no accommodation inside the grounds. Hostels, boutique guesthouses and international hotels cluster in the riverside and central districts, mostly a short ride away.
items.tip: Staying riverside keeps the palace, the National Museum and the night market within walking distance.

items.title: Shops & convenience stores
items.text: Convenience stores and small supermarkets within walking distance cover water, sun protection and basic supplies. Larger shopping centres sit a short drive away in the central commercial district.
items.tip: Small shops still prefer cash — keep low-denomination US dollar notes and some riel for change.

items.title: Fuel & EV charging
items.text: Petrol stations sit mainly on the city's arterial roads rather than in the historic centre. Public electric-vehicle charging is still developing in Phnom Penh, with a limited number of points in service.
items.tip: Drivers and EV users should plan a refuelling or charging stop outside the palace district and allow extra time.

items.title: Money & connectivity
items.text: ATMs and currency-exchange counters operate around the entrance area and the riverside, handling both US dollars and Cambodian riel. Local prepaid SIM cards and eSIM plans are available in the city centre.
items.tip: Admission is paid in cash in US dollars — carry small notes, as card readers are not always available.

items.title: Health & pharmacies
items.text: Pharmacies operate in the surrounding blocks; 24-hour pharmacies and international clinics require a short drive into the central districts. There is no on-site medical facility for visitors.
items.tip: Bring rehydration salts, insect repellent and any regular medication — heat and dehydration are the most common travel complaints here.

items.title: Access, luggage & guides
items.text: Much of the grounds is stone and gravel paving with flights of steps at the Silver Pagoda, so wheelchairs and strollers meet uneven surfaces. Licensed multi-language guides offer their services near the entrance, and left-luggage arrangements are usually informal.
items.tip: Travel light, and ask staff at the entrance which route has the fewest steps on the day of your visit.

seasonal.title: Seasonal Visiting Strategy
seasonal.intro: Climate, crowds and light conditions season by season, so you can choose the right month, the right hour and the right clothing.
seasonal.sourceNote: Climate figures follow the 1991–2020 thirty-year normals published by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information together with Cambodia's Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology. Crowd and light notes describe typical seasonal patterns rather than guarantees.

rows.rain: Very little — roughly 5–25 mm a month
rows.crowd: Peak season, busiest from December to January
rows.light: Clear skies and soft side light in the early morning; long shadows after 15:00
rows.wear: Long trousers or a long skirt with a shoulder-covering top — the dress code applies all year
rows.strategy: The most comfortable window. Arrive at the 08:00 opening, clear the courtyards before the coach groups, and use the 11:00–14:00 closure for a riverside lunch.

rows.temp: 26–36 °C, hottest in April with a higher apparent temperature
rows.rain: Occasional short showers as the monsoon builds
rows.crowd: Moderate, but exceptionally busy around Khmer New Year in mid-April
rows.light: Harsh overhead light at midday; best contrast before 10:00 and after 15:30
rows.wear: Light, loose, pale clothing with a hat, sunglasses and sunscreen
rows.strategy: Split the day around the heat: courtyards from 08:00 to 10:00, shade and fluids through midday, then return in the late afternoon.

rows.rain: 150–250 mm a month, mostly short afternoon downpours
rows.crowd: The quietest months, with September and October the lowest of all
rows.light: Dramatic cloudscapes after rain and strong reflections on wet stone
rows.wear: Quick-drying clothing with a compact umbrella or light rain shell
rows.strategy: Use the dry mornings for the courtyards, keep a waterproof bag for electronics, and stay out of open areas during thunderstorms.

rows.rain: Rain tapering off with occasional showers
rows.crowd: Rising as the dry season approaches
rows.light: Mixed cloud and sun; good diffused light for the murals
rows.strategy: A good compromise: noticeably fewer visitors than peak season, with the grounds green from the rains.

audience.title: Visit Plans by Traveller Type
audience.intro: Three tailored routes — families with children, photographers and nature lovers, and low-mobility visitors who need the flattest paths. Choose by travelling party and the pace you want.

groups.title: Families with children
steps: Start in the shaded courtyards so children can settle before the heat builds.
At the Throne Hall, tell the story of the coronation ceremonies that still take place here.
Turn the Silver Pagoda into a treasure hunt: count the silver floor tiles and find the emerald Buddha.
In the mural galleries, retell the Reamker as a monkey-army adventure.
Finish in the greener riverside space outside the gate to cool down.
groups.tip: Leave before the 11:00 closure and use the entrance-area restrooms first. Strollers cope better with the flat entry paths than with the interior stone steps.

groups.title: Photographers & nature lovers
steps: Be at the gate for the 08:00 opening to shoot the courtyards before the crowds arrive.
Use the morning side light along the Throne Hall facade.
Work the Silver Pagoda steps and gilded spires against the sky.
Move to the cloister for mural details and the play of light and shadow.
Return after 15:00 for warm light on the spires and the riverside promenade.
groups.tip: Photography is restricted indoors: no flash, and tripods and drones generally need permission. Midday hours give the flattest, least rewarding light.

groups.title: Low-mobility & step-free visitors
steps: Ask at the entrance which route has the fewest steps on the day of your visit.
Follow the main axis and its flatter paving to view the Throne Hall exterior.
View the Silver Pagoda from the terrace in front rather than climbing its steps.
Use the shaded seating for a hydration break before continuing.
Finish before the hottest hours and before the 11:00 closure.
groups.tip: Gravel and stone paving make wheelchairs and walking frames difficult in places — bring a companion, water and sun protection, and allow generous time.

routes.title: Recommended Routes (Half Day / Full Day)
routes.intro: Two ready-made itineraries built around the palace's 08:00–11:00 and 14:00–17:00 opening windows and the midday closure.

halfDay.title: Half day · 3 hours
halfDay.label: Morning window

steps.text: Buy your ticket at the main gate and enter as the grounds open.
Cross the courtyards to the Throne Hall and its coronation hall.
Silver Pagoda: the emerald Buddha, the silver-tiled floor and the regalia display.
Mural galleries — the long Reamker cycle along the inner wall.
Ceremonial objects and the French-colonial facades of the inner court.
Final pass through the gardens and the Angkor Wat model.
Exit at the midday closure and walk five minutes to the riverside for an early lunch.

halfDay.note: The whole morning covers roughly 1.5 km of gentle walking within a compact footprint, with shade and benches throughout.

fullDay.title: Full day · 6–7 hours
fullDay.label: Palace plus riverside quarter

steps.text: Palace grounds, Throne Hall and Silver Pagoda in the morning window.
Exit at the closure and walk five minutes to the National Museum of Cambodia.
Lunch in the riverside quarter and rest through the hottest hours.
Return for the afternoon window, or visit Wat Phnom for the city's founding legend.
Stroll Sisowath Quay and the riverside promenade.
Sunset over the four-faced confluence, then the night market for dinner.

fullDay.note: The 11:00–14:00 closure is not dead time — the National Museum next door and the riverside restaurants fill it comfortably.

heritage.title: Understanding the Palace & Visitor Responsibility
heritage.intro: The Royal Palace of Cambodia is a working royal and religious complex rather than a museum set. Knowing what you are looking at — and how to behave around it — makes the visit far richer.

items.title: Naga, garuda and the Khmer cosmos
items.text: Roof ridges and stairways carry naga serpent balustrades and garuda bird-man figures. In Khmer cosmology the naga guards water and earth while the garuda guards the sky, so together they frame each building as a model of the universe.

items.title: The Throne Hall and the coronation tradition
items.text: The tiered roof and gilded spire of the Throne Hall represent Mount Meru, the centre of the cosmos. Coronations, royal audiences and state ceremonies have been held here across successive reigns, and the hall is still in ceremonial use.

items.title: The Silver Pagoda
items.text: Its floor is paved with more than five thousand silver tiles, and its collection includes the emerald Buddha and a gold Buddha studded with thousands of diamonds. It works as the temple of the palace, cared for by monks, rather than as an exhibition hall.

items.title: The painted Reamker cycle
items.text: The cloister wall carries a continuous painted narrative of the Reamker, the Khmer Ramayana. The paintings are meant to be read in sequence, which is why the surface is protected from touch and from flash photography.

items.title: A residence still in use
items.text: Parts of the complex remain the royal residence. When religious or state ceremonies take place, sections close to visitors at short notice — read a closure as a sign of a living institution rather than a poorly run attraction.

legends.title: The widow Penh and the hill of the four faces
legends.text: The founding legend tells of a wealthy widow named Penh who found four Buddha images in the river and raised a hill to enshrine them. The hill became Wat Phnom, and the city took its name from it: Phnom Penh, the hill of Penh.

legends.title: Why the palace stands at this bend
legends.text: The palace overlooks the Chatomuk, the four-faced confluence where the Tonlé Sap meets the Mekong and the Bassac. Traditional Khmer geomancy reads the meeting of waters as a place of power and protection, which is why the capital was moved here from Oudong in 1866.

legends.title: The emerald Buddha
legends.text: The temple of the palace takes its name from its emerald-coloured Buddha image. Comparable emerald figures across Southeast Asia are treated as palladia — protective images on which the wellbeing of a kingdom is said to rest.

legends.title: The naga as water guardian
legends.text: The nagas on the stairways and the many-headed serpent hoods above the doorways recall the Khmer myth of the naga princess and the origin of the royal line, a reminder that the palace stands for sacred as well as political continuity.

heritage.responsibilityIntro: The palace is an active religious and royal site and it belongs to the people who live with it. A few habits keep it open and undamaged for the next visitor.
responsibility: Dress respectfully — shoulders and knees covered — and remove shoes and hats before entering temple buildings.
Keep your voice low, and never lean on, climb or turn your back on Buddha images, naga figures or other sculpture.
Do not touch mural paintings, gilded surfaces or textiles: skin oils and abrasion are the fastest forms of damage.
Flash photography and indoor video are generally not allowed, and drones or professional equipment usually require permission.
Ask before photographing people, monks or worshippers, and step aside during prayers.
Women should avoid touching monks or handing objects to them directly; place items on a surface or pass them via a companion.
Take everything you bring away with you — waste collection inside the grounds is limited.
If a section is closed for a ceremony, accept it quietly: closures protect living traditions rather than inconvenience tourists.

cookie.intro: We use cookies to improve your browsing experience. You can manage your preferences below.

categories.name: Necessary cookies
categories.desc: These cookies are essential for the website to function and cannot be disabled.

categories.name: Analytics cookies
categories.desc: They help us understand how visitors interact with our website by collecting anonymous usage data.
categories.detail: Google Analytics — collects anonymous information about how visitors use our site.

categories.name: Preference cookies
categories.desc: They remember your settings, such as language and theme preferences.
categories.detail: User preferences — saves your language choice and site settings.

categories.name: Marketing cookies
categories.desc: They are used to display relevant advertising and measure the effectiveness of advertising campaigns.
categories.detail: Personalised ads — can show you relevant ads based on your interests.

cookie.consentText: You can change your cookie settings at any time. Please note that disabling certain cookies may affect the functionality of the website.
